title: Torus and tangent dimensions of a semisimple rank-one group
statement:
Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. All subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Assume that $H$ is semisimple: it has no nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, where solvable means that successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Let $S\subseteq H$ be a maximal torus, meaning a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$ and maximal among such subgroups, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Assume that the Krull dimension of $S$ is one [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. There exists an isomorphism of group schemes $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{\sim}S$, and the tangent space at the identity has dimension
$$\dim_F T_{H/F,e}=3.$$
Here the tangent space is the vector space of dual-number points based at the identity [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. No restriction on the characteristic of $F$ is imposed.

source.place: Lemma 20.20, first paragraph of proof, printed p.415: the semisimple rank-one group has dimension 3, and choose an isomorphism from G_m onto its maximal torus. The numerical dimension assertion uses Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (d), pp.412--413. Tangent dimension equals dimension for a smooth group.

proof.text: The subgroup $S$ is nontrivial because $\dim S=1$. Hence $H$ is not solvable: otherwise $H$ itself would be a nontrivial smooth connected solvable normal subgroup. Let $U$ be a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of $H$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable] it has a series $U=U_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq U_n=1$ of closed subgroups, each normal in its predecessor with commutative quotient, so every commutator of $U_a(A)$ lies in $U_{a+1}(A)$. The derived subgroups $D^aU$ exist and are smooth connected by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup], and $D^aU\subseteq U_a$ by induction: the commutator morphism of $D^aU$ is the restriction of that of $U_a$, so it factors through the closed subgroup $D^aU\cap U_{a+1}$, and minimality gives $D^{a+1}U\subseteq U_{a+1}$. Hence $D^nU=1$: $U$ is solvable in the derived-series sense of the statement, and is therefore trivial. Thus $H$ is reductive. By [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer], $C_H(S)=S$ scheme-theoretically. The centralizer is smooth by [lem-sfb-torus-centralizer-smooth-connected], so $S$ is smooth as well. The algebraic-closure hypotheses in these results hold with base field $F$ itself.

source.place: Lemma 20.20, first proof paragraph, p.415; reductivity and centralizers: Proposition 17.61(a), p.372; Proposition 14.21, pp.284--285.

proof.text: Choose a group-scheme isomorphism $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$ provided by the definition of torus in the statement. The tangent vectors at its identity are exactly the tuples $(1+a_i\epsilon)_{i=1}^r$, $a_i\in F$, by [def-sc-gm-ga, def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. Their vector operations are coordinate addition and scalar multiplication: $(1+a\epsilon)(1+b\epsilon)=1+(a+b)\epsilon$ and substitution $\epsilon\mapsto c\epsilon$ sends $a$ to $ca$. Thus the coordinate vectors form a basis and $\dim_F T_{S/F,e}=r$, including $r=0$. Since $S$ is smooth, [lem-sfb-group-tangent-dimension-smoothness] gives $r=\dim S=1$. Inverting the chosen isomorphism now gives $\lambda:\mathbf G_m\xrightarrow{\sim}S$.

source.place: Lemma 20.20, p.415, choice of lambda; Proposition 1.37, p.18; explicit dual-number calculation filling the choice of a rank-one torus coordinate.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety], there is a Borel subgroup $B\supseteq S$, and the Borel variety $X=\mathcal B(H)$ is smooth, connected, projective and nonempty. Its rational points are the Borels, the action of $H(F)$ is transitive, and the stabilizer of $b_B$ is $B$ on all test algebras. In particular $B\ne H$, since $H$ is not solvable. The orbit lemma [lem-sfb-smooth-group-orbit-geometry] gives a smooth locally closed orbit $O$ through $b_B$. It contains every closed point of $X$: closed points are rational by [lem-weil-pbc-closed-point-residue-field-base] and $H(F)$ is transitive. By [lem-sc-lft-over-field-jacobson-space], $O$ is dense in $X$. A dense locally closed subset is open; its closed complement has no closed point and hence is empty by the same density statement. Since $X$ and $O$ are reduced smooth schemes, this is equality of schemes. The orbit identification in [lem-sfb-homogeneous-orbit-quotient-geometry] therefore identifies $X$ with $H/B$.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (a) implies (b) implies (c), pp.412--413; Theorem 17.9, p.354, and the variety of Borels, Section 17f; orbit identification: Propositions 7.11--7.12, pp.141--142.

proof.text: There are at most two Borel subgroups containing $S$. Indeed, [lem-sfb-torus-normalizer-borel-transitivity] says that they are all $nBn^{-1}$ for $n\in N_H(S)(F)$. In the coordinate $\lambda$, [lem-sfb-split-torus-hom-matrices] identifies a group endomorphism of $S$ with $t\mapsto t^m$, $m\in\mathbf Z$. An automorphism has $m\ell=1$ for an inverse exponent $\ell$, so $m=1$ or $m=-1$. If $n_1,n_2$ induce the same automorphism of $S$, then $n_2^{-1}n_1\in C_H(S)(F)=S(F)$ by [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer]. Since $S\subseteq B$, conjugation by this element preserves $B$ on every algebra. Hence $n_1Bn_1^{-1}=n_2Bn_2^{-1}$. Thus the number of these Borels is at most two, in characteristic two as well: the characters $t$ and $t^{-1}$ remain distinct Laurent monomials.

source.place: Theorem 20.16, (a) implies (b), p.412: faithful Weyl action and transitivity; Theorem 12.9(a), pp.233--234, for characters.

proof.text: Put $d=\dim X$. Since $B\subsetneq H$ are smooth connected closed groups, [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] gives $\dim B<\dim H$. The homogeneous quotient dimension formula [lem-sfb-homogeneous-quotient-krull-dimension] gives $\dim H=\dim B+d$, so $d\geq1$. The fixed points of $S$ on $X$ are precisely the Borels containing $S$ by [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety], so step 4 bounds their number by two. Apply [lem-sfb-proper-homogeneous-torus-fixed-bound] to $H/B=X$, which is proper by step 3: it gives at least $d+1$ such fixed rational points. Therefore $d+1\leq2$, and $d=1$. Finally [lem-sfb-borel-quotient-proper-geometry] makes $X=H/B$ integral as well as smooth and proper.

source.place: Theorem 20.16, (b) implies (c), p.413, using Corollary 20.12, p.411; quotient dimension: Proposition 5.23, p.104.

proof.text: The action of $H$ on the smooth proper integral curve $X$ is nontrivial. Otherwise the stabilizer of $b_B$ would be $H$, whereas it is $B\ne H$ by step 3. Thus [lem-sfb-complete-curve-connected-linear-action] gives $X\simeq\mathbf P^1_F$. Transport the action across this isomorphism. The representing automorphism group in [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl], with $r=2$, gives a group-scheme homomorphism $f:H\to\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$: the unit and composition identities of the action give the homomorphism identities. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization], its scheme-theoretic kernel $K$ is a closed normal subgroup scheme of finite type. Every point of $K$ acts identically on $X$ after all base changes, so it fixes $b_B$; the stabilizer assertion of [lem-sfb-general-borel-flag-variety] gives $K\subseteq B$ scheme-theoretically.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (c) implies (d), p.413, using Theorem 20.5 and Proposition 20.7, pp.408--410; kernel: Section 5d.

proof.text: Let $J=(K^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], $J$ is smooth and connected and has the same underlying space as $K^0$. Each $h\in H(F)$ preserves $K$ by conjugation, hence preserves its identity component and its reduced structure. Thus [lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric], with smooth ambient group $H$, makes $J$ normal in $H$ as a subgroup scheme. Also $J\subseteq K\subseteq B$ is solvable: for each integer $a\geq0$, $D^aJ\subseteq D^aB$ by induction, since the commutator on a subgroup is the restriction of the ambient commutator and the derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup containing it. The iterated derived subgroups exist and stay smooth connected by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]. The derived series of $B$ terminates, hence so does that of $J$. Semisimplicity of $H$ now forces $J=1$. Therefore $\dim K^0=0$. By [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates], there are finitely many components of $K$ and all are isomorphic to $K^0$ by translation. Consequently $\dim K=0$. This argument does not require $K$ itself to be reduced or smooth.

source.place: Theorem 20.16 (c) implies (d), p.413, finite-kernel argument specialized to semisimple H; Propositions 1.34--1.39, pp.16--18; derived groups: Propositions 6.18--6.20, pp.129--130.

proof.text: Let $I\hookrightarrow\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$ be the closed image in the factorization of $f$. The kernel-image dimension formula [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image] gives $\dim H=\dim I+\dim K=\dim I$. The closed inclusion gives $\dim I\leq\dim\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$ directly from chains of irreducible closed subsets [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. The group $\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$ of [lem-sfb-projective-frames-pgl] represents the Zariski sheaf quotient of $\operatorname{GL}_{2,F}$ by scalar units; being a scheme it is an fpqc sheaf, so it also represents the fpqc sheaf quotient and is the group $\operatorname{PGL}_{2,F}$ of [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover]. By [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover] with $r=2$, its dimension is $2^2-1=3$. Thus $\dim H\leq3$. If $\dim H\leq2$, then [lem-sfb-connected-group-dimension-two-solvable] would make $H$ solvable, contradicting step 1. The dimensions are finite nonnegative integers, so $\dim H=3$.

source.place: Lemma 20.20, p.415, dimension consequence of Theorem 20.16, p.413; Proposition 5.23, p.104; Corollary 17.27, p.360; PGL dimension from Section 20c.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-group-tangent-dimension-smoothness] to the given smooth affine finite-type group $H$. Equality holds in its tangent-dimension inequality, so $\dim_F T_{H/F,e}=\dim H=3$. Together with the isomorphism $\lambda$ constructed in step 2, this is exactly the two requested conclusions.

source.place: Proposition 1.37, p.18, applied to the dimension computation of Lemma 20.20, p.415.

proof_origin.place: Theorem 20.16, pp.412--413, and Lemma 20.20, first proof paragraph, p.415; Proposition 1.37, p.18. The at-most-two fixed-point bound suffices, and Corollary 17.27 supplies the lower dimension bound.
